rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: Plague is caused by infection with the bacterium Yersinia pestis.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: The organism is usually associated with small mammals and their fleas.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: Plague is not established in the United Kingdom.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: Clinicians with a credible suspected case should seek urgent advice from the UKHSA Imported Fever Service.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: The Imported Fever Service provides round-the-clock advice on risk assessment, immediate management and infection control.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: UKHSA can coordinate urgent polymerase-chain-reaction testing through the Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: All forms of plague are statutorily notifiable in the United Kingdom.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: Preventive advice includes flea-bite protection, avoiding dead animals or infected material, and prompt medical advice after relevant travel.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: Plague risk depends on travel destination, rodent or flea exposure, clinical syndrome, laboratory evidence, contact history and response timing.

rows.source: UKHSA plague epidemiology and imported-case management
rows.verified: Plague evidence is traveller-, exposure-, case-, laboratory-, jurisdiction- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Anthrax is a rare infection caused by the spore-forming bacterium Bacillus anthracis.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Anthrax spores can persist in soil and other harsh environments for many decades.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Human anthrax is very rare in the United Kingdom and has largely been associated with imported contaminated animal products.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Human infection can follow inhalation, ingestion or contamination of damaged skin.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Testing guidance covers clinical specimens, laboratory confirmation and environmental hazards.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Suspected anthrax in an animal should be reported immediately and the animal or carcass isolated.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: A suspect carcass should not be moved, skinned or opened.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Public-health immunisation guidance includes occupational groups whose work creates an increased exposure risk.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Anthrax risk depends on spore source, exposure route, dose, animal or product history, work activity, susceptibility and treatment timing.

rows.source: UKHSA and APHA anthrax recognition, testing and control
rows.verified: Anthrax evidence is animal-, product-, environment-, person-, laboratory- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
